A simple diagram of HIV infection. Left: a round HIV virus particle in cross-section showing the outer envelope with surface proteins, the protein coat (capsid), two strands of RNA and the reverse transcriptase enzyme. Right: a larger CD4 T-helper white blood cell with HIV particles attaching to it, one particle inside, and new HIV particles budding out from its surface. Below, a simple line graph of "CD4 cell count" falling slowly over about ten years, with "HIV in blood" high at first, falling, then rising again, and a shaded section marked "AIDS".

A line graph of antibody concentration in the blood (vertical axis) against time in days (horizontal axis). An arrow at day 0 followed by a small, slow rise and fall in antibody (primary response). A second arrow at a later time followed by a fast, tall and long-lasting rise (secondary response). A dashed horizontal line.

Comparison of Anopheles and Culex mosquitoes in three rows with two columns. Left column Anopheles, right column Culex. Row 1: eggs: Anopheles single eggs with floats; Culex eggs stuck together in a raft. Row 2: larvae: Anopheles larva lying parallel just under the water surface; Culex larva hanging head-down at an angle from a long breathing siphon. Row 3: adults at rest on a wall: Anopheles with its body at an angle of about 45 degrees to the wall; Culex with its body parallel to the wall.

Life cycle of Plasmodium in two halves joined by curved arrows. Left half "In humans": a mosquito biting an arm and injecting sporozoites; sporozoites entering a liver cell; liver cell bursting and releasing merozoites; merozoites entering red blood cells, showing a ring stage, a dividing schizont, and a red cell bursting to release more merozoites; some becoming gametocytes. Right half "In the mosquito": gametocytes taken up in a blood meal, gametes fusing in the stomach, a zygote becoming an ookinete, an oocyst on the stomach wall releasing sporozoites, and sporozoites moving to the salivary glands.

A magnified Cyclops (copepod) viewed from above: pear-shaped segmented body, a single dark eye in the middle of the head, two long first antennae spreading out, short second antennae, swimming legs, a forked tail, and two oval egg sacs at the sides of the abdomen. A small inset of a coiled guinea worm larva inside its body cavity.

Life cycle of Schistosoma haematobium shown as a loop. A person urinating near a pond; spiny eggs in urine falling into water; an egg hatching into a ciliated miracidium; the miracidium entering a small left-coiling Bulinus snail among water plants; many fork-tailed cercariae leaving the snail; cercariae penetrating the skin of a child's leg as he wades in the water; adult male and female worms paired together in a blood vessel near the bladder. A small inset showing a Biomphalaria snail with a flat, disc-shaped shell for comparison.

Life cycle of the blackfly Simulium in a fast-flowing rocky river with white water rapids. Eggs laid on a rock at the water line; larvae attached by their rear ends to a submerged rock, waving fan-like head brushes in the current; slipper-shaped pupal cocoons fixed to the rock with gill filaments; a small dark humpbacked adult fly flying above the river and then biting a person's leg on the riverbank. An inset shows a skin nodule containing coiled adult worms, and tiny microfilariae in the skin.
